edges.description: MSH3 is the obligate partner subunit of MutS-beta, so its absence prevents the complex from assembling.
MutS-beta is the complex that recognises insertion-deletion loops, so losing it removes that recognition step.
MutS-beta carries a second, separate function in homologous recombination, which is lost at the same time.
edges.target: Impaired Homologous Recombination at Structured Break Ends

edges.description: Slippage products left unrepaired accumulate as length changes at repeat tracts.
The same slippage that destabilises repeat tracts genome-wide inactivates APC where those tracts fall inside its coding sequence.
Loss of APC removes the scaffold of the beta-catenin destruction complex.
Unrestrained Wnt signalling in the crypt stem cell compartment produces clonal expansion and dysplastic crypts.
The accumulated dysplastic crypts are the adenomas counted at colonoscopy.
A subset of adenomas progresses to invasive carcinoma as further drivers are hit.

edges.description: Removing Msh3 shifts the somatic Apc mutation spectrum in intestinal tumours from predominantly base substitutions to a mixture in which frameshifts are the majority, which is the mechanistic step this node asserts.

The same cross does not reproduce the polyposis: Msh3-deficient Apc1638N mice show no increase in intestinal tumour multiplicity and no survival difference, where affected people develop multiple adenomas by the fifth decade.
edges.limitations: The mouse proves the molecular step and not the clinical outcome, so it cannot be used to model adenoma burden, age of onset, or the effect of any intervention on polyp count. Mouse Msh6 may cover enough short-indel repair in vivo to keep the residual burden below the adenoma-initiation threshold over a murine lifespan, or the human APC coding sequence may carry more slippage-prone tracts than the mouse orthologue; neither has been tested.

nodes.description: Elevated microsatellite alterations at selected tetranucleotide repeats, present in normal as well as tumour tissue, on a background that is microsatellite-stable by the standard five-marker panel. This is this disease's substitution into the genome-instability hallmark: the caretaker lesion is MutS-beta loss, and the mutator phenotype it produces is tetranucleotide-selective rather than the hypermutation of MutS-alpha-deficient Lynch syndrome, which is why the standard five-marker panel reads stable. The module node binds DNA repair generically; this node binds the specific process whose failure is the mechanism here.

nodes.description: The management recommendation specific to this disease. A published series of biallelic MSH3 carriers proposes colonoscopy every one to two years from age 18 and gastroduodenoscopy at least every five years from age 35, with the interval set by polyposis severity. Note the status of that recommendation: it is the authors' own suggestion from the available cases, not a guideline from a society and not derived from an outcome study in MSH3 carriers, of whom very few are published. The duodenal arm matters because duodenal adenomas are part of the reported phenotype, so surveillance of the colon alone would miss them.

nodes.description: Beyond indel mismatch repair, MutS-beta is required for homologous recombination when double-strand-break ends carry secondary structures, and is recruited to common fragile sites under replication stress. Loss of MSH3 therefore adds a double-strand-break repair deficit to the indel mutator phenotype. Whether this contributes to the extracolonic lesions reported in affected individuals has not been measured.

nodes.description: Without MSH3 the MSH2-MSH3 heterodimer cannot form. MutS-alpha (MSH2-MSH6) is unaffected, which is what separates this disease from the Lynch-syndrome mismatch-repair defects and leaves mismatch-repair protein immunohistochemistry retained.

Insertions and deletions in short repetitive tracts within the APC coding sequence inactivate the gene somatically in colonic crypt stem cells. In adenomas from affected individuals the APC variants are predominantly small deletions, and their enrichment in repetitive sequence context exceeds that seen in APC-driven polyposis. This is the transforming event, and the colonic crypt stem cell is where it happens.
